1. Project overview & objectives

1.1 Context

Netflix's core promise is that every member quickly finds something worth watching. With thousands of titles in the catalogue, personalised recommendations are the main way viewers discover content — they influence what is watched, how long people stay engaged, and ultimately whether members keep their subscription.

1.2 Business question (Challenge 4)

How could Netflix recommend content based on viewer preferences?

I break this one question into five smaller, answerable analytical questions:

# Analytical question Where answered
Q1 Who are the viewers, and what do they declare they like? §6.1
Q2 What do viewers actually do — which titles do they finish, rate, abandon? §6.2 – §6.5
Q3 Do stated preferences (favourite genre) agree with real behaviour? §6.6, §9
Q4 Which recommendation approach is practical for a catalogue where most titles have almost no viewing data (the cold-start problem)? §7
Q5 Does the recommender beat simple baselines, and how sensitive is it to its design choices? §8

1.3 Approach in one paragraph

Because every user has only one viewing record, collaborative filtering ("people like you watched…") cannot work on this data. I therefore design a hybrid, content-based recommender that combines (a) content similarity between a user's taste profile and each title, (b) a quality signal (IMDb rating), (c) a popularity signal based on engagement, plus (d) an exploration bonus for titles nobody has watched yet and (e) a maturity-rating safety filter. The same logic also supports brand-new users using only a declared favourite genre.

1.4 Deliverables produced by this notebook

  • Cleaned and validated datasets with documented assumptions
  • 11 labelled visualisations
  • A transparent, explainable recommender with per-user top-3 lists and a reason for each recommendation
  • Offline evaluation against baselines + sensitivity analysis
  • Business insights, limitations and an action plan

2. Environment setup

All imports are placed in one cell. Constants (file paths, colour palette, reference date, random seed) are defined once so the notebook is reproducible and easy to modify.

Reference date: tenure and "days since" metrics are computed relative to a fixed REFERENCE_DATE instead of today(), so results never change depending on when the notebook is run.

3.1 Data dictionary

users.csv — one row per subscriber

Column Type Description
user_id text (PK) Unique subscriber id, e.g. U001
name text Subscriber name (fictional)
age integer Age in years — used for the maturity filter
gender category Self-reported gender
country category Country of residence
subscription_plan category Basic · Standard with Ads · Standard · Premium
signup_date date Date the account was created
primary_device category Device used most often
favorite_genre category Genre the user chose during onboarding (declared preference)
preferred_language category Interface / audio language preference
avg_weekly_hours float Average hours watched per week

movies.csv — one row per title

Column Type Description
movie_id text (PK) Unique title id, e.g. M01
title text Movie title
primary_genre / secondary_genre category Main and supporting genre
release_year integer Year of release
runtime_min integer Length in minutes
maturity_rating category PG-13 or R
imdb_rating float Public rating on a 0–10 scale (approximate)
language / country_of_origin category Original language and country
director / lead_actor text Key creative credits
netflix_original Yes/No Whether the title is a Netflix Original
tags text Pipe-separated content descriptors (heist|fast-paced)

watch_history.csv — one row per viewing session

Column Type Description
watch_id text (PK) Unique session id
user_id, movie_id text (FK) Who watched what
watch_date date Day of the session
start_hour integer 0–23 Hour the session started
device category Device used for this session
watch_duration_min integer Minutes actually watched
completion_pct float % of the runtime watched
user_rating integer 1–5 (nullable) Explicit star rating — can be missing
rewatch Yes/No Whether this was a repeat viewing
added_to_my_list Yes/No Whether the user saved the title
paused_count integer Number of pauses during the session

ℹ️ The three files are a small illustrative sample created for this assignment (fictional users; real Netflix Original titles with approximate public metadata). They are designed to be realistic enough to demonstrate a full analytics workflow, not to represent Netflix's real member base.

def profile_table(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # One-row-per-column summary: dtype, non-null count, nulls, unique values, example value.
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "dtype": frame.dtypes.astype(str),
        "non_null": frame.notna().sum(),
        "nulls": frame.isna().sum(),
        "unique_values": frame.nunique(),
        "example": frame.iloc[0].astype(str),
    })

Initial observations

  • All three tables have exactly 10 rows, matching the project brief.
  • Date columns (signup_date, watch_date) are loaded as plain text and must be converted to real dates.
  • Yes/No columns (rewatch, added_to_my_list, netflix_original) are text and are better stored as booleans.
  • user_rating is stored as a decimal number although it holds whole stars — this is a side-effect of having missing values in that column (pandas cannot store NaN in an integer column).

4. Data cleaning & quality validation

A recommender is only as good as the data it learns from, so I follow a systematic checklist (the same one I put in the project plan as an early risk-mitigation step):

  1. Completeness — where are values missing?
  2. Uniqueness — are primary keys unique?
  3. Referential integrity — does every foreign key point to a real parent row?
  4. Validity — are values inside plausible ranges?
  5. Consistency — do derived fields (e.g. completion %) agree with their source fields?
  6. Standardisation — trim whitespace, convert types, order categories.

4.1 Completeness — missing values

In [7]
def missing_report(frame: pd.DataFrame, table_name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    report = pd.DataFrame({
        "missing_count": frame.isna().sum(),
        "missing_pct": (frame.isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
    })
    report.insert(0, "table", table_name)
    return report[report["missing_count"] > 0]

missing_overview = pd.concat([missing_report(frame, name) for name, frame in raw_tables.items()])
missing_overview

# Which sessions are missing a rating, and what do we know about them?
watch_raw[watch_raw["user_rating"].isna()][["watch_id", "user_id", "movie_id", "completion_pct", "rewatch", "added_to_my_list"]]
watch_id user_id movie_id completion_pct rewatch added_to_my_list
6 W007 U007 M09 100.00 No Yes
8 W009 U009 M05 92.80 No No

Finding: the only missing values are 2 of 10 explicit ratings (20 %), in sessions W007 and W009. Both of these viewers watched 93 – 100 % of the title — so a missing rating does not mean the viewer disliked it.

Decision: I will not delete these rows (that would throw away 20 % of an already tiny dataset) and I will not fill with the mean rating (that ignores what we know about the session). Instead I derive an implicit rating from completion:

implicit rating=1+4×completion\text{implicit rating} = 1 + 4 \times \text{completion}

so a fully-watched title maps to 5 stars and a title abandoned right away maps to 1 star. In §4.5 I check how well this rule reproduces the ratings that were given.

4.3 Standardisation — types, whitespace and ordered categories

I work on copies (users, movies, watch) so the raw frames stay untouched and any step can be re-run.

In [10]
users = users_raw.copy()
movies = movies_raw.copy()
watch = watch_raw.copy()

# 1) Trim stray whitespace in every text column
for frame in (users, movies, watch):
    for column in frame.columns:
        if pd.api.types.is_string_dtype(frame[column]):
            frame[column] = frame[column].str.strip()

# 2) Convert dates
users["signup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(users["signup_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
watch["watch_date"] = pd.to_datetime(watch["watch_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

# 3) Convert Yes/No flags to booleans
yes_no = {"Yes": True, "No": False}
movies["netflix_original"] = movies["netflix_original"].map(yes_no)
watch["rewatch"] = watch["rewatch"].map(yes_no)
watch["added_to_my_list"] = watch["added_to_my_list"].map(yes_no)

# 4) Ordered categorical for subscription plan (cheapest -> most expensive tier)
PLAN_ORDER = ["Standard with Ads", "Basic", "Standard", "Premium"]
users["subscription_plan"] = pd.Categorical(users["subscription_plan"], categories=PLAN_ORDER, ordered=True)

# 5) Minimum viewer age implied by each maturity rating (used later as a safety filter)
MATURITY_MIN_AGE = {"PG-13": 13, "R": 17}
movies["min_age"] = movies["maturity_rating"].map(MATURITY_MIN_AGE)

print("Converted types:")
display(pd.DataFrame({
    "users.signup_date": [users["signup_date"].dtype],
    "watch.watch_date": [watch["watch_date"].dtype],
    "watch.rewatch": [watch["rewatch"].dtype],
    "users.subscription_plan": [users["subscription_plan"].dtype],
}, index=["dtype"]).T)

4.4 Validity & consistency checks

In [11]
runtime_lookup = movies.set_index("movie_id")["runtime_min"]
recomputed_completion = (watch["watch_duration_min"] / watch["movie_id"].map(runtime_lookup) * 100).clip(upper=100).round(1)
completion_difference = (recomputed_completion - watch["completion_pct"]).abs().max()

signup_lookup = users.set_index("user_id")["signup_date"]
watched_after_signup = (watch["watch_date"] >= watch["user_id"].map(signup_lookup)).all()

validation_rules = pd.DataFrame([
    ("User age is between 13 and 100",                     users["age"].between(13, 100).all()),
    ("Weekly viewing hours are between 0 and 168",         users["avg_weekly_hours"].between(0, 168).all()),
    ("IMDb rating is between 0 and 10",                    movies["imdb_rating"].between(0, 10).all()),
    ("Runtime is positive",                                (movies["runtime_min"] > 0).all()),
    ("Release year is not in the future",                  (movies["release_year"] <= REFERENCE_DATE.year).all()),
    ("Completion % is between 0 and 100",                  watch["completion_pct"].between(0, 100).all()),
    ("Observed user ratings are whole stars 1-5",          watch["user_rating"].dropna().isin([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).all()),
    ("Start hour is between 0 and 23",                     watch["start_hour"].between(0, 23).all()),
    ("Paused count is not negative",                       (watch["paused_count"] >= 0).all()),
    ("Stored completion % matches duration / runtime",     bool(completion_difference <= 0.1)),
    ("Every session happened after the user signed up",    bool(watched_after_signup)),
    ("Every maturity rating has a known minimum age",      movies["min_age"].notna().all()),
], columns=["rule", "passed"])

4.5 Handling the missing ratings (implicit-rating imputation)

In [12]
watch["completion"] = watch["completion_pct"] / 100                      # 0-1 scale
watch["rating_was_missing"] = watch["user_rating"].isna()
watch["implicit_rating"] = (1 + 4 * watch["completion"]).round(2)
watch["rating_filled"] = watch["user_rating"].fillna(watch["implicit_rating"])

# How good is the implicit rule? Compare it against the ratings people really gave.
observed = watch[~watch["rating_was_missing"]]
mean_absolute_error = (observed["implicit_rating"] - observed["user_rating"]).abs().mean()
correlation = observed["implicit_rating"].corr(observed["user_rating"])
print(f"Observed ratings used for the check : {len(observed)}")
print(f"Mean absolute error (stars)         : {mean_absolute_error:.2f}")
print(f"Correlation with real ratings       : {correlation:.2f}")

watch.loc[watch["rating_was_missing"], ["watch_id", "user_id", "completion_pct", "user_rating", "implicit_rating", "rating_filled"]]
Observed ratings used for the check : 8
Mean absolute error (stars)         : 0.53
Correlation with real ratings       : 0.74
watch_id user_id completion_pct user_rating implicit_rating rating_filled
6 W007 U007 100.00 NaN 5.00 5.00
8 W009 U009 92.80 NaN 4.71 4.71

Result: the implicit rule is on average about half a star away from real ratings and is strongly correlated with them, which is good enough for a fallback signal. Rows with an imputed rating are flagged (rating_was_missing = True) so they can be shown differently in charts and excluded from any analysis that requires genuine explicit ratings (e.g. the rating-vs-completion scatter in §6.4).

Why this matters for the business: in real streaming data most members never leave a rating. Recommenders at scale therefore rely heavily on implicit feedback (watch time, completion, re-watches, list adds) — exactly the idea applied here.

5. Feature engineering & master table

New columns turn raw fields into things a recommender (and a business reader) can use.

New feature Table Definition Why it is useful
age_group users <18, 18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45+ Audience segmentation & maturity safety
tenure_years users Years between sign-up and REFERENCE_DATE Loyalty segment
heavy_viewer users Weekly hours ≥ median of all users High-value engagement segment
runtime_bucket movies Short < 120 · Medium 120–139 · Long 140+ min Format similarity & session-length rules
imdb_tier movies ≥ 7.5 acclaimed · 6.5–7.49 well-rated · < 6.5 mixed Quality segmentation
completion_status watch Completed ≥ 90 % · Partial 60–90 % · Dropped < 60 % Satisfaction signal
daypart watch Time-of-day bucket from start_hour Context for ranking
is_weekend watch Saturday / Sunday Context for ranking
engagement_score watch Weighted blend of completion, rating, re-watch and list-add (below) Single "how much did they like it" number that weights the taste profile

Engagement score

engagement=0.50⋅completion+0.30⋅rating−14+0.10⋅rewatch+0.10⋅added to My List\text{engagement} = 0.50\cdot\text{completion} + 0.30\cdot\frac{\text{rating}-1}{4} + 0.10\cdot\text{rewatch} + 0.10\cdot\text{added to My List}

The score lies between 0 and 1. Completion carries the most weight because it is observed for every session; the explicit rating comes second; re-watching and saving to My List are strong but rarer positive signals.

In [13]
# ---------------- users ----------------
users["age_group"] = pd.cut(users["age"], bins=[0, 17, 24, 34, 44, 120],
                            labels=["<18", "18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45+"])
users["tenure_years"] = ((REFERENCE_DATE - users["signup_date"]).dt.days / 365.25).round(1)
users["heavy_viewer"] = users["avg_weekly_hours"] >= users["avg_weekly_hours"].median()

# ---------------- movies ----------------
movies["runtime_bucket"] = pd.cut(movies["runtime_min"], bins=[0, 119, 139, 1000],
                                  labels=["Short (<120)", "Medium (120-139)", "Long (140+)"])
movies["imdb_tier"] = pd.cut(movies["imdb_rating"], bins=[0, 6.49, 7.49, 10],
                             labels=["Mixed (<6.5)", "Well rated (6.5-7.4)", "Acclaimed (7.5+)"])
movies["movie_age_years"] = REFERENCE_DATE.year - movies["release_year"]
movies["short_title"] = movies["title"].str.split(":").str[0]

# ---------------- watch history ----------------
watch["completion_status"] = pd.cut(watch["completion"], bins=[0, 0.6, 0.9, 1.0],
                                    labels=["Dropped (<60%)", "Partial (60-90%)", "Completed (90%+)"],
                                    include_lowest=True)
watch["daypart"] = pd.cut(watch["start_hour"], bins=[0, 12, 17, 21, 24], right=False,
                          labels=["Morning (<12h)", "Afternoon (12-16h)", "Evening (17-20h)", "Late night (21-23h)"])
watch["weekday"] = watch["watch_date"].dt.day_name()
watch["is_weekend"] = watch["watch_date"].dt.dayofweek >= 5

watch["engagement_score"] = (
    0.50 * watch["completion"]
    + 0.30 * (watch["rating_filled"] - 1) / 4
    + 0.10 * watch["rewatch"].astype(float)
    + 0.10 * watch["added_to_my_list"].astype(float)
).round(3)

assert watch["engagement_score"].between(0, 1).all()

5.1 Build the master table (one row per viewing session)

In [14]
master = (
    watch
    .merge(users, on="user_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .merge(movies, on="movie_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
)

assert len(master) == len(watch) == 10, "Join changed the number of rows"
assert master[["name", "title"]].notna().all().all(), "Join produced unmatched rows"
print(f"Master table: {master.shape[0]} rows x {master.shape[1]} columns — no rows lost or duplicated by the joins.")

# Title-level performance, including titles that nobody has watched yet
title_performance = (
    master.groupby("movie_id")
    .agg(views=("watch_id", "count"),
         mean_completion=("completion", "mean"),
         mean_rating=("rating_filled", "mean"),
         total_engagement=("engagement_score", "sum"))
    .reindex(movies["movie_id"])
)
title_performance["views"] = title_performance["views"].fillna(0).astype(int)
title_performance[["mean_completion", "mean_rating", "total_engagement"]] = (
    title_performance[["mean_completion", "mean_rating", "total_engagement"]].fillna(0)
)
movies = movies.merge(title_performance.reset_index(), on="movie_id", how="left")

unwatched_titles = movies.loc[movies["views"] == 0, "short_title"].tolist()
print(f"Titles with zero views (cold-start items): {len(unwatched_titles)} of {len(movies)} -> {unwatched_titles}")

6. Exploratory data analysis (EDA)

EDA answers Q1–Q3: who the viewers are, how they behave, and whether behaviour agrees with what they say they like. Every chart is titled, has labelled axes and uses the same palette.

⚠️ Sample-size note. With 10 users, 10 titles and 10 sessions, patterns are illustrative, not statistically significant. I describe what the data shows and flag where conclusions would need a larger sample.

Reading the chart. The sample covers all four plan tiers, four device types and every age band. The audience is mobile-heavy at the lower-price tiers (Basic and ad-supported users mostly watch on phones) while Premium users all watch on a Smart TV. This matters for recommendations: a phone session is usually shorter and more interrupted than a living-room TV session. One user (Rohan, 16) is a minor — so a maturity filter is not optional.

Reading the chart. Six of ten sessions (60 %) were watched to the end. No viewer dropped a title below 60 % — suggesting that the titles people start are generally well matched to them. 6.5 Do ratings agree with completion? (Visualisation 4)

In [20]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 5.2))

observed_sessions = master[~master["rating_was_missing"]]
imputed_sessions = master[master["rating_was_missing"]]

ax.scatter(observed_sessions["completion_pct"], observed_sessions["user_rating"], s=120,
           color=PALETTE["red"], label="Explicit rating given", zorder=3)
ax.scatter(imputed_sessions["completion_pct"], imputed_sessions["rating_filled"], s=120, facecolors="none",
           edgecolors=PALETTE["charcoal"], linewidths=2, label="Missing → implicit rating", zorder=3)

# Several users share the same coordinates, so label each unique point once with all of its names
point_labels = master.assign(first_name=master["name"].str.split().str[0]).groupby(["completion_pct", "rating_filled"])["first_name"].apply(", ".join)
for (completion_value, rating_value), label in point_labels.items():
    ax.annotate(label, (completion_value, rating_value), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-8, 11),
                fontsize=8.5, ha="right" if completion_value > 99 else "left")

slope, intercept = np.polyfit(observed_sessions["completion_pct"], observed_sessions["user_rating"], 1)
x_line = np.linspace(55, 102, 50)
ax.plot(x_line, slope * x_line + intercept, color=PALETTE["grey"], linestyle="--", label="Trend (explicit ratings only)")

ax.set_xlabel("Completion (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Star rating (1–5)")
ax.set_ylim(0.5, 5.6)
ax.set_title("Visualisation 4 — Explicit ratings vs. completion", loc="left")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

r_value = observed_sessions["completion_pct"].corr(observed_sessions["user_rating"])
print(f"Pearson correlation (completion vs. explicit rating, n={len(observed_sessions)}): {r_value:.2f}")
Pearson correlation (completion vs. explicit rating, n=8): 0.74

Reading the chart. Higher completion goes with higher ratings (positive correlation), which supports using completion as an implicit satisfaction signal when ratings are absent. The two hollow points (Hana and Chloe) are viewers who finished (almost) the whole film yet did not rate it — a reminder that silence ≠ dislike. With n = 8 observed ratings this is directional evidence only.

Reading the chart. All sessions start between 16:00 and 23:00, with a peak around 20:00–22:00 — a classic prime-time pattern. Mobile sessions have the lowest average completion (80 %), Smart TV sessions are in the middle (90 %, dragged down by two long/partial titles) and laptop/tablet sessions are highest (100 % and 96 %, but with only 1–2 sessions each). Mobile viewers also pause more often (3.3 pauses vs. 2.0 on Smart TV, see §6.7). Recommendation lists on mobile could therefore favour shorter, lower-commitment titles, or "resume" prompts.

Reading the chart. The strongest relationships are the ones we would expect: completion_pct, rating_filled and engagement_score move together (the score is built from them), and paused_count moves against completion (r ≈ −0.82: more pauses → less of the film finished). Two other strong values (age ↔︎ tenure_years and age ↔︎ runtime_min) are coincidences of a 10-row sample rather than real effects. Because n = 10, correlations have very wide uncertainty — they are used here to sanity-check the data, not to make claims.

  1. Onboarding genre choices are a reliable cold-start signal and should be used.
  2. Titles must be tagged with more than one genre; a single-genre model would have missed 40 % of the matches.

7. Recommendation strategy — design & implementation

7.1 Strategy overview — a layered ("hybrid") approach

Layer Idea Signal used Strength Weakness
0 · Popularity baseline Recommend what has the highest engagement overall Engagement of all users Simple, no personalisation needed Same list for everyone; ignores unwatched titles
1 · Content-based filtering "More like what you enjoyed" — compare a user's taste profile with each title's features Genres, tags, language, runtime, maturity Works with 1 viewing record per user; explainable; handles new titles Can create a filter bubble
2 · Quality signal Prefer well-reviewed titles IMDb rating Protects against recommending poor titles Rating alone is not personal
3 · Exploration bonus Give un-watched titles a small boost views == 0 Solves item cold-start, increases catalogue coverage Too large a bonus lowers relevance
4 · Business rules Never recommend what was seen; respect age limits Watch history, min_age Safety & user experience —

Why not collaborative filtering? It needs users who share multiple titles. Here each user has exactly one viewing record, so there is no user-user or item-item co-viewing signal. A production Netflix-scale system would blend collaborative and content signals; this notebook shows the content/cold-start half and explains the roadmap in §11.

7.2 Hybrid score

score(u,i)=wc⋅content(u,i)+wq⋅quality(i)+wp⋅popularity(i)+b⋅𝟙[title i has 0 views]\text{score}(u, i) = w_c\cdot\text{content}(u,i) + w_q\cdot\text{quality}(i) + w_p\cdot\text{popularity}(i) + b\cdot\mathbb{1}[\text{title } i \text{ has 0 views}]

with default weights wc=0.60,wq=0.25,wp=0.15,b=0.05w_c=0.60,\; w_q=0.25,\; w_p=0.15,\; b=0.05. Only eligible titles are ranked: not yet watched by the user and allowed for the user's age.

7.3 Step 1 — Describe every title as a numeric vector

Each title becomes a vector made of three blocks, each normalised to unit length and weighted so that the final cosine similarity is a weighted average of the block similarities:

Block Contents Weight
Genre one-hot genres; primary = 1.0, secondary = 0.6 0.50
Tags one-hot descriptors (heist, satire, whodunit…) 0.35
Format language, maturity rating, runtime bucket 0.15
In [25]
# ---------------- model configuration (all tunable parameters in one place) ----------------
BLOCK_WEIGHTS = {"genre": 0.50, "tags": 0.35, "format": 0.15}
SECONDARY_GENRE_WEIGHT = 0.6
DEFAULT_WEIGHTS = {"content": 0.60, "quality": 0.25, "popularity": 0.15}
EXPLORATION_BONUS = 0.05
DECLARED_PREFERENCE_STRENGTH = 0.5     # how strongly the onboarding genre shapes a user's profile
TOP_K = 3

genre_vocabulary = sorted(set(movies["primary_genre"]) | set(movies["secondary_genre"]))
tag_vocabulary = sorted({tag for tag_string in movies["tags"] for tag in tag_string.split("|")})
language_vocabulary = sorted(movies["language"].unique())
maturity_vocabulary = sorted(movies["maturity_rating"].unique())
runtime_vocabulary = list(movies["runtime_bucket"].cat.categories)

feature_names = ([f"genre:{g}" for g in genre_vocabulary] + [f"tag:{t}" for t in tag_vocabulary] +
                 [f"language:{l}" for l in language_vocabulary] + [f"maturity:{m}" for m in maturity_vocabulary] +
                 [f"runtime:{r}" for r in runtime_vocabulary])

def l2_normalise(vector: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    length = np.linalg.norm(vector)
    return vector / length if length > 0 else vector

def build_item_vector(title_row: pd.Series) -> np.ndarray:
    # Convert one movie row into a unit-length feature vector.
    genre_block = np.zeros(len(genre_vocabulary))
    genre_block[genre_vocabulary.index(title_row["primary_genre"])] = 1.0
    genre_block[genre_vocabulary.index(title_row["secondary_genre"])] = SECONDARY_GENRE_WEIGHT

    title_tags = title_row["tags"].split("|")
    tag_block = np.array([1.0 if tag in title_tags else 0.0 for tag in tag_vocabulary])

    format_block = np.array([title_row["language"] == l for l in language_vocabulary] +
                            [title_row["maturity_rating"] == m for m in maturity_vocabulary] +
                            [title_row["runtime_bucket"] == r for r in runtime_vocabulary], dtype=float)

    return np.concatenate([
        np.sqrt(BLOCK_WEIGHTS["genre"]) * l2_normalise(genre_block),
        np.sqrt(BLOCK_WEIGHTS["tags"]) * l2_normalise(tag_block),
        np.sqrt(BLOCK_WEIGHTS["format"]) * l2_normalise(format_block),
    ])

item_matrix = pd.DataFrame([build_item_vector(row) for _, row in movies.iterrows()],
                           index=movies["movie_id"], columns=feature_names)

assert np.allclose(np.linalg.norm(item_matrix.to_numpy(), axis=1), 1.0), "Item vectors must have unit length"
print(f"Item-feature matrix: {item_matrix.shape[0]} titles x {item_matrix.shape[1]} features "
      f"({len(genre_vocabulary)} genres, {len(tag_vocabulary)} tags, "
      f"{len(language_vocabulary) + len(maturity_vocabulary) + len(runtime_vocabulary)} format features)")
item_matrix.loc[["M01", "M03"]].loc[:, (item_matrix.loc[["M01", "M03"]] != 0).any()].T

7.5 Step 3 — Build a taste profile for every user

A user's profile is a vector in the same feature space:

profile(u)=∑jej𝐱j∑jej⏟what they watched, weighted by engagement ej+β⋅𝐠(favourite genre)⏟what they said they like,β=0.5\text{profile}(u) = \underbrace{\frac{\sum_j e_j\,\mathbf{x}_j}{\sum_j e_j}}_{\text{what they watched, weighted by engagement } e_j} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta\cdot\mathbf{g}(\text{favourite genre})}_{\text{what they said they like}},\qquad \beta = 0.5

  • Titles the user loved (high engagement) shape the profile more than titles they only half-watched.
  • The declared genre is the cold-start prior: it is the only information available for a brand-new member.
In [27]
users_indexed = users.set_index("user_id")
movies_indexed = movies.set_index("movie_id")
GENRE_FEATURE_COUNT = len(genre_vocabulary)

def declared_preference_vector(favorite_genre: str) -> np.ndarray:
    vector = np.zeros(len(feature_names))
    vector[genre_vocabulary.index(favorite_genre)] = np.sqrt(BLOCK_WEIGHTS["genre"])
    return vector

def build_user_profile(user_id: str, preference_strength: float = DECLARED_PREFERENCE_STRENGTH) -> np.ndarray:
    history = master[master["user_id"] == user_id]
    engagement_weights = history["engagement_score"].to_numpy()
    watched_vectors = item_matrix.loc[history["movie_id"]].to_numpy()
    behaviour_vector = (engagement_weights[:, None] * watched_vectors).sum(axis=0) / engagement_weights.sum()
    return behaviour_vector + preference_strength * declared_preference_vector(users_indexed.loc[user_id, "favorite_genre"])

user_profiles = pd.DataFrame({uid: build_user_profile(uid) for uid in users["user_id"]}, index=feature_names).T

# Show the strongest 4 features of every profile — a quick explainability check

7.7 Step 5 — Score, filter and rank

score_candidates computes the hybrid score for every title and marks which ones are eligible. recommend returns the top-k eligible titles together with a plain-English explanation — essential for trust and for debugging.

In [29]
def score_candidates(user_id: str, weights: dict = DEFAULT_WEIGHTS,
                     preference_strength: float = DECLARED_PREFERENCE_STRENGTH,
                     exploration_bonus: float = EXPLORATION_BONUS) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Return one row per title with its component scores, final score and eligibility flag.
    user = users_indexed.loc[user_id]
    seen_ids = set(master.loc[master["user_id"] == user_id, "movie_id"])
    profile = build_user_profile(user_id, preference_strength)

    content_similarity = item_matrix.to_numpy() @ profile / np.linalg.norm(profile)
    frame = pd.DataFrame({
        "movie_id": movies["movie_id"], "title": movies["short_title"],
        "content": content_similarity, "quality": movies["quality_norm"], "popularity": movies["popularity_norm"],
        "cold_start": movies["is_cold_start"], "views": movies["views"],
    })
    frame["eligible"] = (~frame["movie_id"].isin(seen_ids)) & (frame["movie_id"].map(movies_indexed["min_age"]) <= user["age"])
    frame["seen"] = frame["movie_id"].isin(seen_ids)
    frame["score"] = (weights["content"] * frame["content"] + weights["quality"] * frame["quality"]
                      + weights["popularity"] * frame["popularity"] + exploration_bonus * frame["cold_start"])
    return frame

def explain(user_id: str, movie_id: str) -> str:
    # Human-readable reason for one recommendation.
    history = master[master["user_id"] == user_id]
    similarities_to_history = item_similarity.loc[movie_id, history["movie_id"]]
    anchor_id = similarities_to_history.idxmax()
    favorite = users_indexed.loc[user_id, "favorite_genre"]
    title_row = movies_indexed.loc[movie_id]

    reasons = []
    if favorite in (title_row["primary_genre"], title_row["secondary_genre"]):
        reasons.append(f"matches your favourite genre ({favorite})")
    reasons.append(f"similar to '{short_title_lookup[anchor_id]}' (similarity {similarities_to_history.max():.2f})")
    if title_row["views"] == 0:
        reasons.append("fresh pick nobody has watched yet")
    return "; ".join(reasons)

def recommend(user_id: str, k: int = TOP_K, weights: dict = DEFAULT_WEIGHTS,
              preference_strength: float = DECLARED_PREFERENCE_STRENGTH,
              exploration_bonus: float = EXPLORATION_BONUS) -> pd.DataFrame:
    scored = score_candidates(user_id, weights, preference_strength, exploration_bonus)
    top = scored[scored["eligible"]].sort_values("score", ascending=False).head(k).copy()
    top.insert(0, "rank", range(1, len(top) + 1))
    top.insert(0, "user_id", user_id)
    top["why"] = [explain(user_id, movie_id) for movie_id in top["movie_id"]]
    return top

all_recommendations = pd.concat([recommend(user_id) for user_id in users["user_id"]], ignore_index=True)
all_recommendations.insert(1, "user", all_recommendations["user_id"].map(users_indexed["name"]))
print(f"Generated {len(all_recommendations)} recommendations ({TOP_K} each for {users.shape[0]} users).")

7.9 Step 7 — Cold-start: recommending to a brand-new member

A new member has no watch history. The recommender falls back to the declared favourite genre (plus quality and the exploration bonus) and still respects the age limit. Three hypothetical new members are shown below.

In [31]
def recommend_new_member(favorite_genre: str, age: int, k: int = TOP_K, weights: dict = DEFAULT_WEIGHTS) -> pd.DataFrame:
    profile = declared_preference_vector(favorite_genre)
    content_similarity = item_matrix.to_numpy() @ profile / np.linalg.norm(profile)
    frame = pd.DataFrame({"title": movies["short_title"], "maturity": movies["maturity_rating"],
                          "content": content_similarity, "quality": movies["quality_norm"],
                          "popularity": movies["popularity_norm"], "cold_start": movies["is_cold_start"]})
    frame["score"] = (weights["content"] * frame["content"] + weights["quality"] * frame["quality"]
                      + weights["popularity"] * frame["popularity"] + EXPLORATION_BONUS * frame["cold_start"])
    eligible = frame[movies["min_age"] <= age].sort_values("score", ascending=False).head(k).copy()
    eligible.insert(0, "rank", range(1, len(eligible) + 1))
    return eligible[["rank", "title", "maturity", "score"]]

for persona, favourite, persona_age in [("Aisha, 19, likes Romance", "Romance", 19),
                                        ("Tom, 14, likes Adventure", "Adventure", 14),
                                        ("Karan, 35, likes Crime", "Crime", 35)]:
    print(f"New member: {persona}")
    display(recommend_new_member(favourite, persona_age).reset_index(drop=True))

8. Evaluating the recommender

8.1 What can be evaluated with 10 sessions?

The classic offline test — hide a title the user watched and see if the model ranks it highly — is impossible because each user has only one record. I therefore use a held-out preference test:

Protocol. Hide each user's declared favourite genre from the model (preference_strength = 0, so recommendations are built only from watch behaviour + quality + popularity). Then check whether the model's top-3 contains at least one title of that genre (hit@3), and what share of all three recommended titles match it (precision@3).

I compare the hybrid recommender against two baselines:

  • Popularity baseline — top-3 eligible, un-watched titles by engagement (the same list for everyone, apart from filtering).
  • Random baseline — expected hit@3 / precision@3 when picking 3 random eligible titles (computed analytically).

Additional non-accuracy metrics capture what good recommenders also need: catalogue coverage, cold-start exposure, intra-list diversity, and safety (zero maturity violations).

In [32]
def recommend_popularity_baseline(user_id: str, k: int = TOP_K) -> pd.DataFrame:
    scored = score_candidates(user_id)
    top = scored[scored["eligible"]].sort_values(["popularity", "quality"], ascending=False).head(k).copy()
    top.insert(0, "rank", range(1, len(top) + 1))
    top.insert(0, "user_id", user_id)
    return top

def expected_random_metrics(user_id: str, k: int = TOP_K) -> tuple:
    # Analytical expectation of hit@k and precision@k for k random eligible titles.
    scored = score_candidates(user_id)
    eligible = scored[scored["eligible"]]
    favorite = users_indexed.loc[user_id, "favorite_genre"]
    matching = sum(favorite in (movies_indexed.loc[m, "primary_genre"], movies_indexed.loc[m, "secondary_genre"]) for m in eligible["movie_id"])
    pool = len(eligible)
    k = min(k, pool)
    hit_probability = 1 - math.comb(pool - matching, k) / math.comb(pool, k)
    return hit_probability, matching / pool

def evaluate_recommendations(recommendation_table: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    enriched = (recommendation_table[["user_id", "movie_id"]]
                .merge(users[["user_id", "favorite_genre", "age"]], on="user_id")
                .merge(movies[["movie_id", "primary_genre", "secondary_genre", "views", "min_age"]], on="movie_id"))
    enriched["genre_match"] = [fav in (p, s) for fav, p, s in zip(enriched["favorite_genre"], enriched["primary_genre"], enriched["secondary_genre"])]

    diversities = []
    for _, group in enriched.groupby("user_id"):
        ids = group["movie_id"].tolist()
        if len(ids) > 1:
            pair_similarities = [item_similarity.loc[a, b] for i, a in enumerate(ids) for b in ids[i + 1:]]
            diversities.append(1 - np.mean(pair_similarities))
    return {
        "hit@3": enriched.groupby("user_id")["genre_match"].any().mean(),
        "precision@3": enriched["genre_match"].mean(),
        "catalogue_coverage": enriched["movie_id"].nunique() / len(movies),
        "cold_start_share": (enriched["views"] == 0).mean(),
        "intra_list_diversity": float(np.mean(diversities)),
        "maturity_violations": int((enriched["min_age"] > enriched["age"]).sum()),
    }

HELD_OUT = 0.0   # preference_strength = 0 hides the declared genre from the model
hybrid_held_out = pd.concat([recommend(u, preference_strength=HELD_OUT) for u in users["user_id"]])
popularity_baseline = pd.concat([recommend_popularity_baseline(u) for u in users["user_id"]])
random_expectation = np.array([expected_random_metrics(u) for u in users["user_id"]])

evaluation_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Random (expected)": {"hit@3": random_expectation[:, 0].mean(), "precision@3": random_expectation[:, 1].mean(),
                          "catalogue_coverage": np.nan, "cold_start_share": np.nan,
                          "intra_list_diversity": np.nan, "maturity_violations": np.nan},
    "Popularity baseline": evaluate_recommendations(popularity_baseline),
    "Hybrid (declared genre hidden)": evaluate_recommendations(hybrid_held_out),
    "Hybrid (production, with onboarding genre)": evaluate_recommendations(all_recommendations),
})

Reading the chart.

  • The hybrid recommender beats both baselines on accuracy: hit@3 of 70 % vs. 42 % (random) and 40 % (popularity); precision@3 of 30 % vs. 16 % and 13 %.
  • Unlike the popularity baseline it recommends titles that nobody has watched (33 % of picks vs. 7 %) and covers more of the catalogue (90 % vs. 60 %).
  • With the declared genre hidden, the hybrid model is already well above random; adding the onboarding genre in production raises precision slightly (30 % → 33 %). With only 10 users, each user is worth 10 percentage points on hit@3, so treat differences of one user as noise.
  • Safety holds: 0 maturity-rating violations in every strategy that applies the filter.

8.3 Sensitivity analysis — how much do the weights matter?

A recommender should not be fragile. I re-run the evaluation with four different weightings of content, quality and popularity and measure (a) accuracy under the held-out protocol, (b) coverage, and (c) how many users keep the same #1 recommendation as the default.

In [34]
weight_scenarios = {
    "Default (60/25/15)":      {"content": 0.60, "quality": 0.25, "popularity": 0.15},
    "Content-heavy (80/10/10)": {"content": 0.80, "quality": 0.10, "popularity": 0.10},
    "Quality-heavy (30/55/15)": {"content": 0.30, "quality": 0.55, "popularity": 0.15},
    "Popularity-heavy (30/20/50)": {"content": 0.30, "quality": 0.20, "popularity": 0.50},
}
default_top1 = {u: recommend(u, k=1, weights=weight_scenarios["Default (60/25/15)"])["movie_id"].iloc[0] for u in users["user_id"]}

sensitivity_rows = []
for scenario_name, scenario_weights in weight_scenarios.items():
    held_out_recs = pd.concat([recommend(u, weights=scenario_weights, preference_strength=HELD_OUT) for u in users["user_id"]])
    metrics = evaluate_recommendations(held_out_recs)
    top1_now = {u: recommend(u, k=1, weights=scenario_weights)["movie_id"].iloc[0] for u in users["user_id"]}
    same_top1 = np.mean([top1_now[u] == default_top1[u] for u in users["user_id"]])
    sensitivity_rows.append({"scenario": scenario_name, "hit@3": metrics["hit@3"], "precision@3": metrics["precision@3"],
                             "coverage": metrics["catalogue_coverage"], "diversity": metrics["intra_list_diversity"],
                             "same_#1_as_default": same_top1})
sensitivity_table = pd.DataFrame(sensitivity_rows).set_index("scenario")

Findings.

  • The content-heavy setting stays close to the default (80 % of users keep the same #1 pick, same hit@3) because the personalised signal dominates.
  • The popularity-heavy setting changes the most top picks (only 20 % keep their #1) and lowers hit@3 from 70 % to 50 % — giving popularity too much weight erodes personalisation.
  • The quality-heavy setting performs worst (hit@3 of 20 %, coverage 60 %): it pushes the same highly rated dramas to everyone.
  • The default is a sensible compromise; in production these weights would be tuned through A/B testing (see §11).

Reading the chart. Two findings. First, content similarity alone already surfaces unwatched titles — even with no bonus, 8 of the 30 picks (27 %) are titles nobody has watched, something a popularity ranking can never do. Second, the exploration bonus acts as a dial: 0.05 adds one more cold-start pick (30 %), while 0.15 lifts the share to 40 % but starts to push these titles into lists where their content match is weak (and reduces the number of different titles recommended from 9 to 8). This is exactly the knob a product team would tune with an A/B test.

1. Device-aware ranking
   Evidence : Mobile sessions finish 80% of a title on average vs. 93% on other devices.
   Action   : Rank shorter / lower-commitment titles higher on mobile and show 'continue watching' prompts.

2. Cold-start is a catalogue problem
   Evidence : 3 of 10 titles (30%) have zero views. Only 7% of popularity-baseline picks are such unwatched titles, versus 30% for the hybrid recommender, which also covers 90% of the catalogue (popularity: 60%).
   Action   : Keep an exploration bonus so new titles receive their first views; monitor coverage as a KPI.

3. Use onboarding genres + multi-genre tags
   Evidence : Declared favourite genre matched actual viewing for 10 of 10 users, but 4 of them match only via the secondary genre.
   Action   : Always collect onboarding genres and tag every title with several genres.

4. Silence is not dislike
   Evidence : Users who skipped the rating watched 96% of the title on average (rated sessions: 87%).
   Action   : Treat completion, re-watch and My List as first-class implicit signals; never count a missing rating as negative.

5. Maturity guardrails are essential
   Evidence : 60% of the titles are R-rated; the youngest user (16) can access only 4 of 10 titles.
   Action   : Apply age/profile filters before ranking, and make sure the teen catalogue is rich enough to avoid an empty home screen.

6. Lower-tier plans watch less
   Evidence : Premium users average 12.6 h/week vs. 7.8 h for other plans (7.2 h for ad-supported).
   Action   : Target onboarding and re-engagement recommendations at ad-supported / Basic users to lift hours watched.

7. Prime-time dominates
   Evidence : 90% of sessions start between 17:00 and 23:59; partial sessions were: Red Notice, The Irishman, Bird Box, Don't Look Up.
   Action   : Refresh the home page ranking in the late afternoon; surface shorter titles late at night.

9.1 Insight summary

# Business insight Why it matters to Netflix
1 Context changes completion — mobile viewers finish less of a title. A "same list for every device" approach wastes mobile sessions; context-aware ranking raises completion and satisfaction.
2 Popularity-only recommenders starve new titles — cold-start titles never get a first audience. New content (and the money spent on it) stays invisible; an exploration bonus and coverage KPI fix this.
3 Declared preferences work as a cold-start signal, especially with multi-genre tagging. Faster time-to-first-good-recommendation for new members reduces early churn.
4 Implicit signals are richer than ratings. Only a minority of members rate titles; completion, re-watch and list-adds fill the gap.
5 Maturity filters are mandatory and the teen catalogue is much smaller. Brand safety, regulation and parent trust.
6 Premium viewers engage more than other tiers. Recommendations can be used as a lever to raise engagement and retention on lower-priced and ad-supported plans.
7 Viewing is concentrated in the evening. Time-aware refresh of recommendations.

9.2 KPIs to monitor if the strategy were launched

KPI Definition Direction Why
Click-through rate (CTR) on recommendation rows Plays started ÷ titles shown ↑ Relevance of what is shown
Completion rate Sessions with ≥ 90 % watched ÷ sessions ↑ Satisfaction after the click
Time-to-first-play Seconds from opening the app to starting a title ↓ Reduced browsing friction
7-/30-day retention Members still active after 7/30 days ↑ Business outcome
Catalogue coverage Share of titles recommended at least once ↑ Return on content investment
Intra-list diversity 1 − average similarity within a list Keep stable Avoid filter bubbles
Cold-start conversion New titles that reach N views in 14 days ↑ Success of exploration
Safety violations Titles shown that violate the profile maturity limit = 0 Trust and compliance

10. Limitations, risks & ethics

Area Limitation / risk How I would address it
Sample size 10 users × 10 titles × 10 sessions is too small for statistical tests; correlations and group averages are illustrative. Re-run the same notebook on a larger export — the code is parameter-free with respect to data size.
One session per user No collaborative filtering possible; offline evaluation limited to a held-out preference test. Collect ≥ 5–10 interactions per user; add leave-one-out evaluation and matrix factorisation.
Synthetic user data Users are fictional; real behaviour is noisier. Validate on real (anonymised) data before drawing business conclusions.
Evaluation circularity Declared genre is used both as a prior and (in held-out mode) as ground truth, so accuracy is only partly independent. Use real engagement outcomes (plays, completion) in an online A/B test.
Filter bubble Content-based recommenders tend to repeat what a user already likes. Monitor diversity; add a "serendipity" slot.
Fairness & privacy Age, gender and country are sensitive; profiles can be misused. Use age only for safety filtering; do not use gender in ranking; follow GDPR-style data minimisation.
Tiny candidate pool Each user has only 3–7 eligible titles, so lower-ranked slots are partly "filler" (e.g. a high-quality drama shown to an action fan with low content match). In production the pool is thousands of titles; use a minimum content-match threshold before filling a slot.
Imputed ratings The implicit rating rule is approximate (≈ 0.5-star error). Treat imputed values as weak signals and flag them in the data.

11. Recommendations & next steps

11.1 Recommended strategy for Netflix (answer to the business question)

  1. Start with a hybrid content-based recommender (as built here): it works from day one for new members and new titles, is explainable, and respects age limits.
  2. Collect implicit feedback aggressively (completion, re-watch, My List, pauses) — ratings alone are too sparse.
  3. Make recommendations context-aware — device and time of day change which titles will actually be finished.
  4. Reserve exploration slots so new titles get their first audience and the catalogue is fully used.
  5. Layer collaborative filtering on top once users have several interactions — blend it with the content score.

11.2 Roadmap

Phase Action Success measure
Now Deploy content-based hybrid to a small test cohort CTR and completion above popularity baseline
Next A/B test the weights (content / quality / popularity / exploration) Higher 30-day retention, stable diversity
Later Add collaborative filtering and sequence models (what to watch next) Improved hit-rate on held-out plays
Later Context features (device, time, weekday) as ranking inputs Higher mobile completion

12. Final conclusions

Business question: How could Netflix recommend content based on viewer preferences?

Answer. Netflix should recommend through a layered hybrid strategy that (1) builds each member's taste profile from what they actually watch and finish (engagement-weighted), (2) uses the genres they pick at onboarding as a cold-start prior, (3) balances relevance with quality and popularity, (4) deliberately exposes unwatched titles through an exploration bonus, and (5) always applies maturity safety rules.

What the analysis showed

  • Data quality was high — keys unique, foreign keys valid, all 12 validation rules passed. The only gap (20 % missing ratings) was handled with an implicit rating derived from completion, which tracks real ratings to within about half a star.
  • Behaviour matches stated taste: every user watched a title in their declared favourite genre — but 4 of 10 only via a secondary genre, so multi-genre tagging matters.
  • Context matters: mobile sessions have the lowest completion; all viewing is in the evening.
  • The hybrid recommender is better than the baselines on what matters: above random accuracy, broader catalogue coverage, exposure for titles nobody has watched, and zero maturity violations.
  • The design is robust: content-heavy and default weightings give almost the same top picks, while popularity-heavy weightings reduce personalisation.

Honest caveat. The dataset is tiny and partly synthetic, so these results demonstrate a method rather than prove business outcomes. The method, however, is fully reusable: replace the three CSV files with larger exports and every step in this notebook runs unchanged.

Skills demonstrated: data loading and inspection · validation and cleaning · missing-value strategy · feature engineering · merging relational tables · exploratory analysis with 11 visualisations · building and evaluating a recommender · translating results into business actions.

    "Joins preserved all 10 sessions":                          len(master) == 10,
    "Item vectors have unit length":                            bool(np.allclose(np.linalg.norm(item_matrix.to_numpy(), axis=1), 1.0)),
    "Every user received 3 recommendations":                    bool((all_recommendations.groupby("user_id").size() == TOP_K).all()),
    "No user was recommended a title they already watched":     bool(not all_recommendations.merge(watch[["user_id", "movie_id"]], on=["user_id", "movie_id"]).shape[0]),
    "No maturity-rating violations in recommendations":         evaluation_table.loc["maturity_violations", "Hybrid (production, with onboarding genre)"] == 0,
    "At least three business insights derived":                 len(business_insights) >= 3,
}
for description, passed in final_checks.items():
    print(("✔ PASS  " if passed else "✘ FAIL  ") + description)

assert all(final_checks.values()), "At least one final check failed"
print(f"\nAll {len(final_checks)} checks passed — notebook executed successfully from top to bottom.")
